4. 
Loper Bright—a Proposed Framework, The Loper Bright opinion 
appears to take the position that, if a court can give meaning to a legal text, it 
should do so without “deference” to agency judgments. But the Court 
acknowledges that some statutory schemes authorize agencies to “regulate 
subject to the hmits imposed by a term or phrase that leaves agencies with 
fLexibihty,’ . . . such as ‘appropriate’ or ‘reasonable.’ ” What the majority 
appears to mean by this claim is that terms like “appropriate” or “reasonable” 
lack a single determinate meaning discernible by using the ordinary tools of 
construction. In that sense, they are truly “ambiguous.”
If that is the meaning of this passage of Loper Bright, then the opinion 
has ultimately drawn the line between ambiguity and legal meaning in a 
different place than Chevron did—at the point at which the line would be 
drawn in those cases not involving an agency. Agency action pursuant to terms 
like “reasonable” then would be subject to arbitrary and capricious review 
under the State Farm standard.
In addition, the Court repeatedly refers to the notion of “respect” under 
Skidmore as the appropriate standard for courts to apply. But the Court also 
observes that “interpretations issued contemporaneously with the statute at 
issue, and which have remained consistent over time, may be especially useful 
in determining the statute’s meaning.” Whether there is daylight between 
Skidmore and this latter articulation remains to be seen.
Lastly, the Court observes that some statutes “expressly delegate[ ]” to an 
agency the authority to give meaning to a particular statutory term, citing, for 
example, 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(15), which exempts from provisions of the Fair 
Labor Standards Act “any employee employed on a casual basis in domestic 
service employment to provide companionship services for individuals who 
(because of age or infirmity) are unable to care for themselves (as such terms 
are defined and delimited by regulations of the Secretary}!' It appears that 
statutes that expressly incorporate a delegation using language of this sort 
confer some degree of executive discretion on those who implement them.
